blocks.text: A strain-gauge rig on a crane hook logs 20 000 readings in one test. You need the peak reading, the readings above a safety limit, and the data from one channel only. Writing a loop for each request is slow and error-prone; array indexing answers all three in a single line.

blocks.markdown: An **array** is a block of numbers of one type stored in a grid. A one-dimensional array is a *vector*; a two-dimensional array is a *matrix* with rows and columns. This unit uses Python with NumPy, where indices start at **0** and `a[i]` is the $(i+1)$-th element. Three skills cover most engineering data handling: building evenly spaced vectors, slicing out pieces of a matrix, and selecting values with a condition.

blocks.title: Evenly spaced vector
blocks.text: `np.linspace(a, b, N)` returns $N$ points from $a$ to $b$ **inclusive**, so there are $N-1$ equal intervals. `np.arange(a, b, h)` steps by $h$ and **excludes** $b$. Use linspace when you know the end points and the number of samples.

blocks.caption: Step size and sample positions of np.linspace(a, b, N).

blocks.title: Evaluating a function over a range
blocks.prompt: Evaluate the deflection-like function $y(x)=2x^2+1$ (x in metres, y in millimetres) at five equally spaced points from $x=0$ to $x=1$ m.

steps.text: Create the grid with `x = np.linspace(0, 1, 5)`. Here $N=5$, so there are 4 intervals.
Compute the step: $h=(1-0)/(5-1)=0.25$ m, so the vector is [0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0].
Apply the formula to the whole vector with `y = 2*x**2 + 1`. NumPy squares each element, multiplies by 2 and adds 1, giving $y_k = 2x_k^2+1$ at every point.
Check one point: at $x=0.75$, $2(0.5625)+1=2.125$, which matches the fourth entry.

blocks.markdown: **Slicing** selects a sub-array using `start:stop:step`, where `stop` is excluded. For a matrix, give one slice per axis: `A[rows, cols]`. A lone colon `:` means 'all'. Negative indices count from the end, so `-1` is the last element. A slice of the form `A[1, :]` returns a single row as a 1-D array.

headers: Result shape for a 4x4 matrix A
blocks.caption: Common slices of a 4x4 matrix. The stop index is never included.

steps.text: `A[:,2]` takes column index 2 from every row: [12, 22, 32, 42].
`A[1:3,0:2]` takes rows 1 and 2 (stop 3 excluded) and columns 0 and 1: [[20, 21], [30, 31]].
`A[::2,::2]` takes rows 0 and 2 and columns 0 and 2: [[10, 12], [30, 32]].

blocks.markdown: A **boolean mask** is an array of `True`/`False` values the same shape as the data, produced by a comparison such as `P > 40`. Indexing with the mask, `P[P > 40]`, keeps only the elements where the mask is `True`. Combine conditions with `&` (and), `|` (or) and `~` (not), and wrap each comparison in parentheses because `&` binds more tightly than `>`.

blocks.title: Selecting overloaded readings
blocks.prompt: Five member loads in kN are `P = [12, 48, 35, 60, 27]`. Find the loads above 40 kN, their positions, and the loads between 30 and 50 kN.

steps.text: Build the mask: `P > 40` gives [False, True, False, True, False].
Apply it: `P[P > 40]` returns [48, 60]. Two readings exceed the limit, and `np.sum(P > 40)` counts them as 2 because `True` counts as 1.
Combined condition: `(P > 30) & (P < 50)` gives [False, True, True, False, False], so `P[...]` returns [48, 35].

blocks.answer: Above 40 kN: [48, 60] kN at indices 1 and 3; between 30 and 50 kN: [48, 35] kN.

items: Use `np.linspace` when the number of points matters; use `np.arange` when the step matters.
Slice with `start:stop:step`; the stop index is excluded.
Index matrices as `A[rows, cols]`, one slice per axis.
Make masks with comparisons and combine them with `&`, `|`, `~` and parentheses.
Use `np.where(mask)` to recover the indices of the selected elements.

blocks.title: Views versus copies
blocks.text: A basic slice such as `A[0:2,:]` is a **view**: assigning into it changes the original array. A boolean-mask selection such as `A[A>5]` makes a **copy**. Writing `a[(a>2) and (a<5)]` raises an error because `and` cannot compare whole arrays; use `&`. Also, `np.arange(0, 1, 0.1)` may or may not include rounding-affected end points, so prefer `linspace`.

points: np.linspace(a, b, N) gives N points including both ends with step (b-a)/(N-1).
Slices A[r, c] use start:stop:step with the stop excluded and zero-based indices.
Boolean masks select by condition; combine them with & | ~ and parentheses.
Basic slices are views; mask selections are copies.

distractorRationale.c: Correct: five points, step 0.5, both ends included.
distractorRationale.a: This divides by N=5 instead of N-1=4 and so never reaches 4.
distractorRationale.d: This steps by 1 and ignores the end point 4.
distractorRationale.b: This starts one step late; the first point must equal the start value 2.

questions.explanation: linspace includes both end points and uses N-1 = 4 intervals, so the step is (4-2)/4 = 0.5. The points are 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4.

questions.stem: A probe is traversed along a 0.30 m duct and positions are generated with `np.linspace(0, 0.30, 7)`. What is the spacing between adjacent positions, in metres?
questions.explanation: Seven points create six intervals, so the spacing is 0.30/6 = 0.05 m. Dividing by 7 would be the common error.

questions.stem: A wall temperature profile is $T(x)=400-1500x$ (T in kelvin, x in metres). Positions are `x = np.linspace(0, 0.2, 5)`. What is the value of `T[3]` in kelvin? Indices start at 0.
A matrix `B` has shape (5, 5). What is the shape of `B[1:4, ::2]`?

distractorRationale.c: Counts the rows as 4 by wrongly including the stop index 4.
distractorRationale.b: Counts only 2 columns, forgetting that index 0 is included with ::2.

questions.explanation: The row slice 1:4 selects indices 1, 2, 3, which is 3 rows. The column slice ::2 selects indices 0, 2, 4, which is 3 columns, giving shape (3, 3).

questions.stem: A data array `A` has 6 rows and 3 columns. Which expression returns its last column as a 1-D array of length 6?

distractorRationale.d: This extracts the last row (length 3), not the last column.
distractorRationale.c: Column index 3 does not exist in a 3-column array, so it raises IndexError.
distractorRationale.b: This selects only the last row's last element, giving length 1.

questions.explanation: The first slice `:` takes all rows and `-1` selects the last column. `A[-1, :]` would give the last row, and `A[:, 3]` raises an IndexError because valid column indices are 0 to 2.

questions.stem: Strain readings in microstrain are `e = np.array([120, -15, 340, 95, 410, -60])`. What does `e[e > 100]` return?

distractorRationale.b: Correct: the values satisfying the condition.
distractorRationale.c: This is the mask itself, not the result of indexing with it.
distractorRationale.a: These are the indices of the selected values, which np.where would return.

questions.explanation: The mask `e > 100` is [True, False, True, False, True, False]. Indexing with that mask returns the values at True positions: 120, 340 and 410.

questions.stem: Wind speeds in m/s are `v = np.array([3.2, 7.8, 5.1, 9.4, 6.6, 8.0])`. Compute the mean of `v[(v > 5) & (v < 9)]` in m/s.
questions.explanation: The mask keeps 7.8, 5.1, 6.6 and 8.0 (9.4 and 3.2 are excluded). Their sum is 27.5, and the mean is 27.5/4 = 6.875 m/s.

questions.stem: A student writes `a[(a > 2) and (a < 5)]` to select values of a NumPy array strictly between 2 and 5 and gets an error. Explain why it fails, give a correct expression, and state whether the result is a view or a copy.
markingGuide: `and` requires a single truth value, but a comparison on an array yields an array of booleans, so the truth value is ambiguous
Parentheses are needed because `&` has higher precedence than the comparison operators
Mask indexing returns a copy, not a view, so changing it does not alter `a`
questions.explanation: Python's `and` tries to reduce each array to one boolean, which NumPy refuses. The element-wise `&` combines the two masks position by position, and the result of mask selection is a new array.

questions.stem: If `S = A[0:2, :]` is a basic slice of matrix `A`, then assigning `S[0, 0] = 99` also changes `A[0, 0]`.
questions.explanation: Basic slices are views that share memory with the original array. Writing through the view therefore modifies the original data.

questions.stem: A force log is stored in a NumPy array `D` of shape (100, 4) whose columns are time, Fx, Fy, Fz. Write slicing expressions to obtain (i) the Fy column for all steps, (ii) the three force columns for the first 10 steps, and (iii) every fifth time step with all columns. State the shape of each result.
markingGuide: Recognises zero-based indexing and that the stop index is excluded
questions.explanation: Column 0 is time so Fy is index 2. The row slice :10 gives 10 rows, 1: gives the 3 force columns, and ::5 over 100 rows gives 20 rows.
